title: Noting
hookLine: the Burmese method made well-known by Mahasi Sayadaw: "rising, falling," "hearing," "thinking"

lines: A QUIET VOICE FOR YOUR MIND.
cards: Rebound. A sports commentator doesn't argue with the play or daydream about next season. The voice just names what's happening, a half-step behind the action.
Now turn that voice inward and make it quiet, barely a whisper. Hearing. Thinking.
Itching. Wanting. That's close to a meditation method now taught around the world, and it came out of a meditation center in Yangon, in Myanmar.

teach.b: The teacher was Mahasi Sayadaw, a Burmese monk and scholar; Sayadaw is a Burmese title for a senior teacher.

The prime minister of newly independent Burma invited him to lead a meditation center in the capital, and lay people came in large numbers to learn his method. Here it is. Put your attention on the belly.
As it rises with the in-breath, note silently: rising. As it falls: falling. When something else takes your attention, note that instead, simply and lightly: hearing, hearing.
Walking works the same way: lifting, moving, placing, with each step.

Mahasi taught it as a way to live out an instruction in the Satipatthana Sutta, which this path walked through a few weeks ago: when walking, know that you're walking; when standing, know that you're standing.

teach.h: A SOFT NOTE, A LIGHT TAP.
teach.b: The note is not the point. Teachers say the label should be soft, most of the attention on the experience itself, like a finger tapping each moment on the shoulder: this one, now this one.
Done steadily, it shows yesterday's three marks up close.
Everything noted is already changing. Not every teacher uses labels. Some find them helpful for a busy mind; others find they get in the way and prefer bare awareness without words.
Teachers in his line say: use the note while it helps, drop it when it doesn't.

how: In Mahasi-style centers in Myanmar and around the world, meditators alternate sitting and walking periods for most of the day, noting 'rising, falling' and whatever else arises, and report to a teacher regularly.

games.q: you're noting 'rising, falling' and a dog starts barking outside. what's the instruction?
o: ignore it and force attention back to the belly.
note 'hearing, hearing', then return to rising, falling.
stop and go close the window.
games.why: whatever takes your attention gets noted, lightly, and then you return to the belly.

practice: Rest a hand on your belly if that helps, and silently note rising as it rises, falling as it falls. When a sound pulls you away, note hearing, hearing; when a thought comes, thinking, thinking; then back to rising, falling.
Keep the note a whisper and the attention on the feeling itself.

wordCard.voice: Noting. Mahasi Sayadaw's method: softly naming each moment of experience, starting with the belly, rising, falling.

orig.note: Pali sati: mindfulness, the awareness that noting is meant to support.

carryVoice: Your line: rising, falling. A soft note, a light tap, and back to the belly. Day two hundred ninety-seven, done.
